# OrgPath × SQL Server — The Integration Bridge {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important appearance="default"}
## Status — Draft bridge between two draft anchors
Both endpoints of this bridge are pre-acceptance. The
[SQL Server Identity Transformation](index.qmd) series is **DRAFT v0.1** and its
governing decision **ADR-091** is **PROPOSED**; the
[UIAO OrgPath](../orgpath-narrative/index.qmd) series is the explanatory
companion to substrate canon (`ADR-035`–`ADR-040`, `ADR-048`). Treat the
integration patterns here as the seam these two series share, not as accepted
normative governance, until ADR-091 is accepted and both series are reviewed
against it.
:::

The two reading sequences on this portal that most often get read in isolation
are siblings. The [UIAO OrgPath](../orgpath-narrative/index.qmd) series builds a
governance substrate; the [SQL Server Identity Transformation](index.qmd) series
consumes it. Read apart, each is complete. Read together, they describe a single
movement: an Active Directory forest's organizational structure becomes a set of
Entra ID attributes, and those attributes become the access-control authority for
a SQL Server estate that no longer trusts the domain. This page names the seams
where the two meet, corrects the one place the relationship is most often
described wrongly, and proposes the order to read them in.

## The substrate and the consumer

OrgPath is the organizational coordinate system Microsoft's identity stack does
not supply on its own. The OrgPath series develops it across seventeen documents,
beginning with what the native stack provides and ending with the synthesis; the
implementation itself — populating the Entra ID attribute lineage from HR data —
is the subject of [OrgPath Book 04](../orgpath-narrative/Book_04.qmd),
"Implementing OrgTree and OrgPath." Everything downstream depends on Book 04
being done.

The SQL Server series consumes that coordinate system at exactly one structural
point: access control. [SQL Book 07](Book_07_CPT_01.qmd), "AD Group Types and the
Entra Perimeter," is where a migrated SQL Server stops being governed by AD
security groups maintained through helpdesk tickets and starts being governed by
Entra dynamic security groups whose membership is computed from OrgPath
attributes. The dependency direction is therefore fixed: the OrgPath attribute
infrastructure must precede the SQL dynamic-group access work, not the reverse.

## The five seams

| # | Seam | SQL side | OrgPath / canon side |
|---|------|----------|----------------------|
| 1 | **Dynamic-group access** | Book 07 — OU-derived groups become OrgPath dynamic groups | `ADR-036` dynamic-group model; `ADR-078` facet schema; `dynamic-groups.yaml` |
| 2 | **DBA delegation** | Book 07 Ch 2 — Administrative Unit delegation | `ADR-037` Administrative Unit provisioning |
| 3 | **Migration sequencing** | Book 02 consolidation + ADR-091 §1 gate | OrgPath Book 04 coverage maturity |
| 4 | **Conditional Access perimeter** | Book 07 — the binary outer perimeter | OrgPath-derived groups + CA (`ADR-008`) |
| 5 | **Closure & drift** | ADR-091 §5 — CCM-BIR closure artifact | OrgPath drift engine (`ADR-040`, `UIAO_163`) |

### Seam 1 — Dynamic-group access (the one most often described wrongly)

This is the load-bearing seam, and it is worth stating its mechanism precisely,
because it is easy to get wrong. OrgPath is **not** a single packed string stored
in one attribute. It is a multi-facet schema (`ADR-078`) materialized across
several Entra `extensionAttribute` slots — region, department, division,
clearance, account-type, and the rest — and a dynamic-group rule is composed from
**per-facet predicates**, not from a string comparison against a whole path. The
canonical rules are not hand-authored `New-MgGroup` calls; they are **rendered**
by the dynamic-group library from
[`src/uiao/canon/data/orgpath/dynamic-groups.yaml`](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/data/orgpath/dynamic-groups.yaml)
against the active per-facet Codebook (`UIAO_151`), under `ADR-036` and
`ADR-084`. SQL Book 07's worked example — a single-facet rule that admits a
principal whose OrgPath attribute matches and whose title contains "DBA" — is an
illustrative slice of that general model, not the whole of it. Any integration
artifact that hardcodes a single `extensionAttribute` holding a `path=...` string
is describing a shortcut the substrate does not take.

### Seam 2 — DBA delegation

Once SQL access rides on Entra groups, the people who manage those groups need a
scope. [SQL Book 07 Chapter 2](Book_07_CPT_02.qmd) puts DBA-team membership
management inside an Administrative Unit so a DBA can manage the SQL groups for
their branch and nothing else. That Administrative Unit is the OrgPath-shaped
delegation surface `ADR-037` provisions — the same branch structure that drives
the dynamic-group rules also bounds who may edit them.

### Seam 3 — Migration sequencing

ADR-091 §1 makes estate consolidation a **gate** in front of engine-layer auth
migration: an instance is migrated only after it is classified retain or
consolidation-target ([SQL Book 02](Book_02.qmd)). OrgPath coverage is the second
gate on the same instances. A business unit whose OrgPath attributes are not yet
populated cannot have its SQL access expressed as dynamic groups, so migration
waves follow **both** the consolidation classification **and** OrgPath coverage
maturity. The series do not assert calendar dates for this; ADR-091's own plan is
anchored to the program's 2027-04-01 NTLM backstop, not to fixed quarters.

### Seam 4 — Conditional Access perimeter

Book 07 closes on the architectural dividend: once every SQL login is a type-E
login backed by an Entra principal, Conditional Access becomes a **binary** outer
perimeter — device compliance, Named Locations, sign-in risk — that a single
surviving Windows login would bypass entirely. The principals that perimeter
evaluates are the OrgPath-derived groups; the CA design that governs them is the
same one the OrgPath series develops as the cloud successor to GPO logon
restrictions ([OrgPath Book 15](../orgpath-narrative/Book_15.qmd)). The two
series describe one perimeter from two sides.

### Seam 5 — Closure and drift

ADR-091 §5 defines the CCM-BIR per-instance record as the closure artifact for
Transformation #7 — `LoginMode = 1`, zero type-S/W/G logins, `sa` disabled,
Arc + Managed Identity healthy, CA-MFA satisfied — and makes closure
**continuously verified**, not a point-in-time claim. That continuous posture is
where the substrate's own drift discipline (`ADR-040`, `UIAO_163`) closes the
loop: an OrgPath drift on a SQL-governing dynamic group is not a cosmetic event,
it is a change in who can reach the database, and it surfaces as a
Transformation #7 compliance signal rather than disappearing into manual group
management.

## Recommended reading order

The two series interleave; reading either straight through leaves the seam
implicit. This order makes the dependency explicit.

| Step | Read | Why here |
|------|------|----------|
| 1 | OrgPath Books 01–04 | Understand the substrate and **build it** (Book 04 is the attribute-population prerequisite) |
| 2 | SQL Books 01–03 | The authentication inheritance, estate consolidation, and the discovery audit |
| 3 | SQL Books 04–06 | The Arc identity bridge, the login migration, NTLM elimination at the SQL layer |
| 4 | **SQL Book 07** ←→ OrgPath Book 04 | **The seam** — dynamic-group access and the Conditional Access perimeter consume the substrate from step 1 |
| 5 | SQL Books 08–10 | The upstream application chain, the transformed steady state, and the ADCS → Cloud PKI dependency |
| 6 | OrgPath Book 15 | The substrate synthesis as a capstone, now that you have seen a consumer end-to-end |

## What this bridge deliberately does not claim

For the avoidance of doubt, and because earlier external syntheses of this
relationship got these details wrong:

- It does **not** claim OrgPath lives in a single `extensionAttribute` as a
  packed path string. OrgPath is a per-facet schema (`ADR-078`) across multiple
  attributes, and rules are composed from per-facet predicates (`ADR-036`).
- It does **not** prescribe hand-authored `New-MgGroup` commands as the way to
  create SQL access groups. The canonical groups are rendered from
  `dynamic-groups.yaml` against the Codebook and extended by governed PR.
- It does **not** assign fixed calendar-quarter milestones to the integration.
  Sequencing is gated by consolidation classification and OrgPath coverage, with
  the program's 2027-04-01 NTLM block as the only fixed date in the plan.

## Companion canon

- [ADR-091](/docs/adr/adr-091-sql-server-authentication-transformation.html) —
  SQL Server Engine Authentication Transformation (the engine-layer decision the
  SQL series motivates; **PROPOSED**).
- `ADR-036` — Dynamic Group Provisioning (the OrgPath-driven Entra security-group
  model SQL Book 07 consumes).
- `ADR-037` — Administrative Unit Provisioning (the delegation surface for DBA
  group management).
- `ADR-078` — OrgPath Attribute Schema (the multi-facet attribute model).
- `ADR-040` / `UIAO_163` — the drift engine that makes OrgPath-on-SQL changes a
  compliance signal.
- `UIAO_135` §3.2 — Transformation #7 (the gap ADR-091 closes).
